editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I am Tom Swope, and I am submitting this oral history on behalf of World War II veteran Gabriel Andrasovsky. Mr. Andrasovsky served in the U.S. Army with the 45th Division, 179th Regiment, First Battalion. He served in Sicily and Italy, and his highest rank was buck sergeant. Mr. Andrasovsky and his son recorded this interview during March of 2003 at Gabriel's home in Parma, Ohio, and asked me to submit it to the Veteran's History Project. Gabriel was 81 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Okay. My name is Al James Andrasovsky, and better known in the entertainment world as Al James, the magician. But right now the star of our tape here is my father, Gabriel Andrasovsky. And he is going to tell us some stories about things that happened to him when he was fighting in World War II.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: First of all, I guess you were wounded at Venafro. Is that how you pronounce the name?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Venafro.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: All right. Where is Venafro?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Venafro is -- it is somewhere east of -- of Salerno. No. It is a little more high up than Salerno. It is that city up there, that big one, for crying out loud.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Well, anyway. It is in Italy; right?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. Near Naples.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Okay. It is in Italy. All right. Near Naples maybe?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Naples. Yes.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. All right. Let's do Naples. Anyway, tell us the story. Tell us how you got wounded.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: How I got wounded?

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Well I was digging a fox hole. I tried to dig a fox hole up there. I was up on the -- in the hills. And we got clay. I got down about eight inches and it was nothing but clay down there. And there is no way you are going to dig with a little two-foot long -- that is how big here. Bigger is, you know. And you -- you can't get into clay like that. That is as hard as heck, that clay. So I couldn't dig the fox hole down. So I thought I -- I would just dig it as deep as I can and then a long one I will have instead of a little round one that is deeper. So I started digging on that thing. Then all of a sudden ___ it came in. There was a little tiny tree about -- about six, seven feet high like a big bush but it had had a pretty -- a lot of it there. And that is where that -- the mortar shell hit. It was an 81-millimeter mortar shell that come in. And it slammed me right in the left elbow. And I thought, sure as heck, I am going to lose my arm down there from the elbow down. And I picked my arm up with the other hand and moved it around and it didn't feel like it was busted up. But I got that slammed with a shrapnel. So I got that -- there were guys in the little -- little barn about 50 feet away from me. That is all. And I went in -- went in there and they -- they bandaged it up pretty good. And then from there, of course, I went to the hospital, you know.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: How long did it take you to recuperate?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: It took about a month.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: A month to recuperate?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. A good -- a good month. Because it was -- yeah. It was November the 9th. And then by -- coming up near Christmas, I was all set.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: So you got a purple heart for that; right?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Oh, yeah. You get a purple heart for that. And I am getting right now $104 a month for it. And I tell all of my buddies, Boy, if I knew this, I would have stuck my hand up a lot sooner.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. Really. But what is interesting is you had what, three -- three of your brothers and sisters were all in the service during World War II; is that right?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: And all four of you got purple hearts; isn't that correct?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. We all got purple hearts. But my sister, of course, it was given to her when her husband got killed in the war. She didn't get hurt.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: But they do send her the purple heart. But the other two brothers were -- they got -- they got hurt.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Henry was in Palolo -- Palolo Islands where he got hurt on a beach. And my brother Frank was stuck with -- he was stuck with frozen feet. That is what he got. He didn't -- he didn't get any shots or anything like that.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: But he was in a prisoner of war camp, though; right?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. He was in a prisoner of war camp but he escaped from there. And that is when he had to go. And it was early in February and cold as hell. And it took him six days and nights to get back to the lines. What he did is he listened for the artillery and he knew where the artillery was hitting in that direction. And that is where the front lines are going to be. So that is how he got back. Six -- six days it took him to get back. And he had frozen feet when he got back in there. And they did not get him real badly hurt, or anything. His legs were okay after a while. And that is how his purple heart worked.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Now, I want you to tell us a story about how you landed on a beach somewhere in Italy and what happened.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Well, when we hit Anzio, the big deal about Anzio was that we had left the enemy, who had us really trapped down below because there was a big field there wide open a mile wide and we couldn't get across that mile-wide field because they were up -- up on a hill. At the end of this there was a hill. And they knew we would not be firing at them because that is where they -- the Italians taught their priests to be priests. It was a school for priests. Yeah. And -- and we couldn't shoot any artillery up at the enemy because we would be hitting the priests, too. So what -- the only thing we had to do is we pulled out of there, went back to Naples, got on a boat and we went up and around the enemy, in back of them. That is when we hit Anzio, the beach. That was a biggie, a real good one for us. So we were behind the enemy. They had to run like hell to get out of there. They had to go sideways, too, not just straight back because we were in back of them. They had to run towards the other side and go all around. And that -- that got us all going again back up, back up. Yeah. And it didn't take too long where I saw the -- from Anzio, got a little bit up north of Anzio. And I can see big buildings out there, you know. And I asked one of the Italians that were out there and he said that is Rome. So that is Rome. We never got -- I never got that far with them. I got -- in the next three or four months, I got my malaria. That stopped a heck of a lot. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Very good. Now, I think there is a story about how a major helped you carry your rifle because you had a lot of heavy things to carry and the major ended up shooting off his thumb by accident with your rifle, I guess. Why don't you tell us that story.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. He was pretty darn good because every time I carried my walkie-talkie for Company A while they -- there was a lieutenant there. He would always take my rifle and give it to one of the GIs to carry it for me because I had a 15-pound walkie-talkie on my back for them, you know, to use.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: You were a radioman?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. I was a radioman. And this time, I don't know why -- how we got a major, Major Spradling. Major Spradling took my rifle and he carried it for me. Real nice. Now, we went up to this city called Venafro, and we were there for two nights right near the city. And, finally, we got out of there. We were going downhill. And the major is carrying my rifle. And he -- but he got his thumb over the barrel there sticking out. Now, we -- we were going downhill, and it had rained the night before and it was kind of sloppy walking down. And, all of a sudden -- now, that major is about 15 feet away from me on the left side going down. And two airplanes came, German planes, came. Now, we had a lot of woods there. There wasn't real big woods but there was enough that we weren't afraid of airplanes because we saw they had no bombs under the wings. If they had bombs under the wings, it would worry us a little bit, you know. They wouldn't have to hit you with it. You get shot at about 30 feet away from you, too. Well, these planes came past us. And I see my -- the major. He unlocked the rifle and he is pointing it up trying to get it pointed up at one of them two planes but he couldn't because there are too many trees, and stuff, and he just couldn't get a good look at them to fire it. So whatever. Then about five minutes later, we are going -- walking down the hill. Them planes left. They just kept going somewhere. And, all of a sudden, I hear a bang. And I looked to the left of me and he is laying down. What he did, he slipped and the -- my rifle slammed into a tree and it set it off. He didn't have his hand on it by the trigger to do it. It is just that big bounce -- big bounce it shot the thing off. And he had his thumb over the barrel again. And, boy, he -- the first thing he said, he said, I shot my thumb off with this rifle. He was mad at the rifle. I was scared he was going to be mad at me. But -- well, he should have given it to one of the GIs there like the other guys did all of the time. Or he forgot to lock it again once them planes left. Yeah. That was too bad. That is Major Spradling. He shot his thumb off. And I felt so sorry for him. God, he was a hell of a good guy trying to help me out like that.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: All right. Now, when you were in the hospital, after you started to get a little bit better, they sent you to recuperate at a place that was like some kind of like a villa or a palace. Why don't you tell us about that?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. It was a palace. It had -- it had four stories, and it was just one big red brick building about -- I would say it had to be at least 200 feet long, at least. Yeah. And we were on one end of it upstairs on the fourth floor. And it was -- we were just recuperating now. We -- we are not hurting. We could walk around and do whatever we want to out there. So that was a hell of a nice place. They had nurses over there living in the front -- the front of the yard. This palace was back about 200 feet back to the street. And the nurses had a couple of little houses up near the -- near the street. And we had to go down and down to the other end of it to eat all of the time, which wasn't bad because we had an elevator. It was a cute elevator. You pull one string and it took you down and up, up and down. Yeah. And then it was like a rehab. It was -- that is really what it was, a rehab. We took over a palace. The United States took over that building and kept it for a rehab. That was really nice.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Kind of luxurious?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: It is in -- it is in Caserta. Caserta. That is not far from Naples, too. That is -- I don't think it is 40 miles from Naples, the city Caserta.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Did it have a swimming pool?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: I don't know. I don't know if it had a swimming pool.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: It was a beautiful place, though?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Oh, yeah. It was such a beautiful building. Boy. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Very good. All right. Let's see. Now, a -- of course, a lot of entertainers like to go out and entertain the troops when there is a war going on.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: I can't think of her name.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. There is quite a few that I guess you saw. Humphrey Bogart and Joey Brown and Frances Langford.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Frances Langford.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: And people like that. Why don't you tell us about some -- tell us about some of the shows that you saw.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. We saw a nice show. After the Sicilian campaign was over, we kicked the enemy off the island and we went to see Bob Hope and Frances Langford. And I think the guy's name was Antonio, or something, that played a -- what do you call them things?

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Accordion?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. He played the accordion for Frances Langford when she sang. And we went to see them there. That was real -- real good. That was funny as hell, too, everything. They build a stage for him, for Bob Hope and the girl, you know, and they had it at the bottom of a slight hill. So we all sat down on the hill. And, you know, if you are right in back of the guy in front of you, you can see real good. It was real sharp. I was in about the fourth row. That is right. It was real good. And, yeah, Frances Langford sang really, really nice. And what surprised me, later on, when I was in Caserta, they had -- they had Frances Langford and another girl come out. And they put us in different rooms, small rooms, about eight of us sitting on -- on two beds. And we were -- and Frances Langford come in and she sang and the other girl danced a little bit and the guy played music. And this girl got through dancing. She came in and she sat down right next to me. And Frances Langford sang that song. I forget what it is again. But, anyways, this girl put her arm around. Oh, yeah. She put her arm around me and she sang in my ear to the same tune that Frances Langford was singing except she made a real carny, a good juicy one, different words. Yeah. It was real cute. I had a laugh like hell at her. Yeah. That was pretty good. There was one thing we saw there. Yeah. We saw Joey Brown. I forget even what -- all of the things he did there except one thing he was saying he was practicing to be a pitcher and the way he did it, he wound up and he, like, threw the ball. You know, he didn't have anything in his hands, really. Threw the ball. And he went (making sound) and then he looked way up in the sky and way in back of him. The guy hit a home run, you know.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. Right. Very good.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: That is something. We saw him. And we saw Humphrey Bogart. We saw Humphrey Bogart when we were waiting to go to Anzio later on. Yeah. And -- yeah. He said he just got through -- he just left Rick's Cafe the other day, he said, because he was right there.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Casablanca?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. Casablanca. He was -- he said he left Rick's Cafe. And it was -- it was a pretty good show with him doing it. And his wife, her name is what? She ain't that movie star that he married a couple years later. It was a funny name. Margo.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Margo?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: I am pretty sure it was Margo, his wife's name was Margo. And when the thing was over, I thought, I'd love to get his autograph. They said he is going to sit down at a table and give autographs out. So this buddy -- buddy of mine said he will -- come with me because he wants to get a picture. And I had my camera with me. So I took my camera with me, naturally. We went over there and we were just around in a circle in back of where the thing was. And there were -- they had a big, big tent there and that is where Humphrey Bogart and his wife were staying in that tent. And they had a little table outside of there. And there was a line of guys, about a hundred of them or 200, of guys waiting, they were all in line waiting to get autographs. And he is sitting there. He autographed everybody. And he looked up at us. And we were standing about 20 feet away from him watching him. He looked up at us a couple of times and he said, Hey, you guys want to take my picture? And we said yeah. And he said okay. And he ran in and got his wife Margo out, comes back out and he puts his arms around her, you know, and they both smile and we took pictures of them. Now, the pictures, we had to -- I had to turn in my -- what do you call it?

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Film?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: The what?

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: The film?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. I had to turn the film in to be developed, you know. And it took about three weeks. I had got it back, a lot of pictures, there was not one picture of Humphrey Bogart in there. And at least he could have had that -- what do you call it?

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: The negative?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: The negative. If he would have just sent me the negative back I could get it done somewhere else. And that damn fool. Why didn't he make more pictures and then send me some?

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. Right.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: He could have made 20 pictures and sent me one. I would have been happy. And he is a noncombatant up there in England somewhere besides, that son of a gun.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. Right.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: He had a lot of nerve not to do that.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Right. How many times did you have malaria?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Three times I had it.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Where did you get it the first time?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: First time I got it was at Anzio. Yeah. And it was -- we were there sometime around -- near the end of May, I think. No. The end of April. Near the end of May. It was near the end of May that I got malaria. And what I didn't know, I was on rotation on June 1st.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: What does that mean?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: They send you home.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Oh, you were supposed to go home?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. They send you home. And -- well, they said rotation but they never brought anybody back. They send -- they send everybody home and left them home. And they didn't tell anybody that he is going home at the end of the month because when it started about four -- three months before that, they told the lieutenant we had there, lieutenant, that he is going home I think, like, it was March 1st. And he wrote a lot of people that he knew, his friends, his families, his girlfriend, that he was going to be home, he is on rotation. Three days later he got killed.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: So they stopped telling anybody who is on rotation that he is, that he is on rotation. They -- they pick you up on the first of the month, first day of the month, and tell you you are going home. Boy, good surprise.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. Right.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: That is what happened when I had the malaria. And they give you 13 days no matter how good you get. If you are there three days and you are -- you are got -- your malaria is solvent, or something, you still have got to be there 13 days. It is a --

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: It is a rule?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. You have got to have it. So when I -- when I got out of there, it was about 10 days into May already or into June, I think. Yeah. It was towards the end of May, into June. And I was going back to my outfit, and I stopped at the regimental headquarters to find out where my outfit was. And the guy asked me my name. I told him. Gabe Andrasovsky. He said, Oh, you are Sergeant Andrasovsky. We have been looking for you. He said, Where the heck were you all this while? I told him I was in two different places. We were in one -- one tent and then for two days and then they moved me to another tent. He said, That is why we couldn't find you. I said, Well, it didn't hurt. He said, Well, you are on rotation. And I almost died. I sat down quick. Boy, I am on rotation. So I asked him where my buddies were, where my outfit was and he told me how to get there. They took me on a Jeep. And I gave them all of the canned -- I had a lot of good canned food that I got off -- out of the tents. I went to see the chiefs over there, and everybody, and they gave me a lot of good cans of food. But I gave them all to my buddies there. I was the sergeant in the section, radio -- radio chief. I was in the radio section at that time. And, yeah, they loved it. I gave them all of that good food. And I went back, and we went home. And the day I got home to my house, eight o'clock in the morning I got home and my -- my girlfriend lived next -- across the hallway from our -- from our room. And I had called her up and told her I was going to be home at eight o'clock so she wouldn't go to work on that Saturday. And she stayed home and waited for me. At ten o'clock I got malaria. Two hours later I got malaria again. I couldn't even walk. I had to lay down on a couch and whatnot. And I found out where I had to go. And her brother -- her brother was home at that time, George. George died a week -- a little over a week ago, by the way, Frank.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Oh, I didn't know that.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. George died. George had a car with him, and he drove me up to Crile Hospital it was called. And I had to be there 13 days. So I was there 13 days. And then 15 days was my -- my whatever you call it they give you, stay home. Yeah. I was home almost a month. It was a hell of a good one.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: That Crile Hospital, that is the place that is Cuyahoga Community College now; right?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Which is where I graduated from. So that is a coincidence.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: I know.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: You were at a hospital that eventually became a college that I graduated from.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: That is a coincidence.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. Crile Hospital.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: So that is two bouts of malaria. And then you had another one?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. I had one more. When I went back -- when I went back to the -- in the Army to a -- where was it in camp -- I forget the name of the camp. It was in New Jersey. And I was there about one week. And I got malaria again. That was the third one. That was the last one I had, too. I didn't get another one.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Okay. Very good.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: That was a big reason that they sent me up to Missouri. And while I was there in Missouri, they told me I was getting out of the Army, they were dispatching me. That was pretty good. And that was the day they also, on the way out, we got -- I had a meeting with some people that called me and they were American -- them AAA guys, or whatever, A

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. They talked to me and saw everything I had and they said they are going to put me in for getting some money for having malaria and that wound.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: And that was a good thing they did that because then I -- I got -- I am still getting money.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. Right. And let's see. One more question about -- who was the officer who was on the front lines with you? Was it that major?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Major Spradling.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. Anything more you want to say about him?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: The only time I saw Major Spradling -- I never heard of him before that. And after that, I never saw him until I was going home because I went -- they sent me back to Naples, and I went and I found out that one of my men was in the hospital. He had got shot in both legs. And I wanted to see him. J. D. Simpson from Oklahoma. He lived in -- next to Oklahoma City. And I went to see J. D. He was in the hospital over there. And he told me Major Spradling was in something down below working. And I went to see Major Spradling, too, but I didn't tell him who I was. I just walked in and I didn't want him to know that I was the guy that it was my rifle's fault that he got so hurt. He didn't recognize me because he only saw me that one day.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. Right.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Uh-huh. And I didn't want to tell him who I was. I just talked to him a little bit. And I noticed he did not have a thumb.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. Right. Wow.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Okay. Any more stories about the war? Have you got any more stories?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. I have got a long one maybe. I don't know if it is too long, or what. But when we were sent -- it ain't so long, maybe. I hate to tell people about some of it. Well, they had me and Dick Adams -- Dick Adams was my corporal. I was at --

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Sergeant?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. I was a sergeant and he was with me. And they send us -- they said, We want you guys to go down with the walkie-talkie.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Okay. Go on with your story.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Okay. They wanted to send a couple of guys down and -- at night. And they said, You have to send them down to -- as soon as they hit the first street to stop and listen to see what kind of -- are there trucks or are there tanks over there, or whatever, and call us up, take a radio with you and call us up and let us know what you are hearing down there. So I went with Dick. Dick Adams, he was from -- he is from south -- right under Chicago.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Gary, Indiana?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: No. No. He is under Chicago.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Oh. Like Blue Island?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Blue Island. He was -- he is from Blue Island, Illinois.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Suburbs of Chicago?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. Adams. And he and I went -- it started we went, of course, about 10 o'clock at night. It was dark, you know. We are going down through the woods. And the moon -- the moon was shining like hell. And it was a little bit on the low side, too. That moon was so doggone bright we were glad we were going through woods. And we -- I don't know. We walked about 10, 15 minutes, at least, going down. We were afraid that we were getting out of -- out of our lines. And you couldn't tell anything, especially. And we came to -- we were on the left side of this forest. We looked over there and there was a wall about 10 feet high, a high wall made out of rocks. And it went down as far as we could see it. And the moon was on the left. And there was a nice shadow from this -- this wall. So we were walking down in the darkness in the shadow. And, boy, you won't believe this. We come to the end it. I could see the end of it because the light shined over there. We could see the end of it. And we were coming down. And I don't know. Adams, he come a little closer to me because he was standing way pretty far out on the right side where he was almost into the light. And I -- I am carrying my -- my -- my gun at port arms right in front of me. And I have got my bayonet on it, also, all set. And I come around that corner and what I can see about six feet from me there is a German guard, it has got to be a guard. And his rifle is on his shoulder. He has got it on his shoulder. I have got mine like this. I walked around and pointed and in a half a second you do everything you had to do right. I slammed right into him with my -- with my --

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Bayonet?

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: -- bayonet because I didn't want to fire my rifle. You could see everything right away that that is a guard, there is hundreds of guys all along somewhere there sleeping. And they come out every five minutes to check their guard. Man, I -- all I did, I took about three or four steps as fast as I could and run right into him. And I know I think he just started to look to see me, whatever, when I caught him and I think he tried to duck because I -- I had -- I had it out going right -- right -- I hit him right in the stomach with the bayonet so I don't miss him. And I caught him in the throat. I know that. I caught him in the throat. And I knocked him backwards and fell right on him. And Dick Adams, he said, Hey, that is a guard, we have got to get out of here. I got up and run like hell after that because he is running when he said that for the -- for the woods. The woods were only about 50 feet away, see, where he started. Boy, I run after him and we were running through them woods and going up and it is -- we are glad it is a little bit darker in the woods and we are going up there running for it. We must have been running for about five or ten minutes, and a big light went -- they shot up one of them damn things. So they -- they had found the guard then already. Oh, man, was it bright up there and in back of us yet. And where we were it wasn't so bad. It was dark enough that we could still be running. And that light went out. It lasted about two minutes. That is all. And they shoot up all of them damn things all in one big thing. It burst open. And we were -- while we were running, we are tripping on stuff, we are tripping on any -- any kind of things that is down there and falling into trees, bumping trees. Now, at this -- they put a second flare up and it was closer to us this time. And it still -- it wasn't bad at all. But here is what happened. Dick Adams, he looks back at me, you know, and he just says, Boy, it is bright here. He says, Where the hell is your rifle? I almost died. I didn't have it. When I got up, I just run like hell with him. And that is a hell of a thing for a -- to do, a guy that needs a rifle and you leave the damn thing laying down there with -- oh, boy. So I never -- when we kept going, I told him, I left it over there, I guess. I said, Don't tell anybody what happened. Nothing. Nobody. We will just tell them that we saw guards and we run back. So we did that. And he didn't -- he was good. He didn't tell anybody I left the rifle over there.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Imagine that. We got back and we didn't -- we didn't say a hell of a lot to the lieutenant. We had a new lieutenant then. Yeah. The other one, I don't know where they put him. I forgot his name. Yeah. I know his name. Conforty. And somebody told us that his name was Conforteni and he changed it when he got in the Army to Conforty, took the n-i out. I don't know. Pretty good.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: So you finally told the world that you lost that rifle. So you are probably going to get a bill from the Army now for that rifle.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Okay. And then you had another story you wanted to tell.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. Just a little bit. It ain't such a big deal. But when we hit Salerno, that was the first time that the Americans, and all, hit Europe. It was at Salerno on September 9th, 1943. November 9th is when I got hurt over there, come to think of it. Everything happened on the 9th because we hit -- July 9th we hit Sicily. And September the 9th we hit Europe and we hit Italy. And we were on an LCI, landing craft infantry. It is a small ship with maybe 150 people on it, or so. And I noticed there was one -- one of the sailors there, he was about a six-and-a-half-foot tall guy. And in those days, when we saw a six footer, we used to say, Boy, that guy is a six footer, you know. But this guy was a lot bigger than that. And we talked to him every once in a while going over there. And, finally, we were going to hit the beach at Salerno. And it was, well, very early in the morning. It was dark outside, real dark. It was about, I don't know, three o'clock in the morning, or something. And the boat had two ramps, one ramp on each side of it, that went down into the water. And I went on the right side in back of one guy, was holding his shoulders so I know where I am, and I can hear somebody up in front of us saying, Don't swim, don't swim, don't swim. I was wondering what the heck is going on. So we are going down and we -- it didn't take that long. We get down, and the guy in front of me, I lost him because he -- he went off the ramp. And I heard somebody saying, Don't swim. And I took my last step. I was holding my hand up on my back and holding my radio up there. And I stepped off the ramp. I went down into the water. The water was about a foot over my head. And, all of a sudden, somebody grabbed me and lifted me up, moved me about four feet forward and he said, Don't swim. And it was -- there happened to be a hole right where that ramp was and the rest of it was about two feet higher than that hole. And they had that big guy over there standing there. I know that had to be him, that big sailor. And he was up on all of the guys on that thing there saying, Don't swim, don't swim. And we got to the beach and I had to throw -- I threw my gas mask. You have a gas mask off when you are hitting beaches. And you just throw it away if you don't need it, don't have to put it on. And they find out a hell of a lot of them are piled up over there by the time it is over. But that was funny. Yeah. That was Salerno when we hit Europe.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: All right. So now you have another story about something that happened to you in combat.

sp.speaker: Gabriel J. Andrasovsky
sp.p: Yeah. It was funny, sort of. Yeah. We were going through -- through the left edge of the forest and I happened to look out to the left. About 200 yards away was the hills. And I looked on top of that hill. I could see two Germans. And I know they were Germans. You could see by their helmet. They are Germans. They come up over the top of that hill and slid right down in back of some bushes. Now, they are pretty far away, and all. But, still, that ain't too far. I told my lieutenant right away what I saw. I said, See them bushes up there where that one is a little heavier than that one? They slid right back over there. He says, Well, I can't even tell which ones you are talking about. And he called a guy over with the BAR rifle. He said, I want you to fire it right at where you think they are. So they put a little thing in there. It has got 20 rounds. And they brought -- brought the -- what do you call it -- the tripod. Brought me a tripod and put it down, put the rifle on the tripod and I laid down on the ground. And I just fired it right down the line where I -- where I knew they were. I don't know if I hit anybody, you know. Not anything. But I fired the 20 rounds all -- all across there. So maybe -- maybe I hit somebody. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Al James Andrasovsky
sp.p: Uh-huh. All right. So those are some of the war stories of my father here. Again, his name is Gabriel Andrasovsky. And his current address is 8301 Sierra Oval in Parma, Ohio, and in an area that they call Dogwood Estates. So, anyway, those are the stories, and I hope you find them very interesting. My name is Al James Andrasovsky, and I want to thank you for listening.
